checks.what_the_results_show: K01 (F01): per_core avg_response rose from 0.889 (C01) to 4.972 (C02), +459%, far above the 25% threshold, and it rose in every seed (0.92/0.92/0.83 to 5.33/5.25/4.33). Global stayed at exactly 0.889, inside the 5% band. per_core was worse than global in C02. K03 (F02): a larger quantum raised per_core avg_response further, 4.972 to 8.722. No result challenges H01 in the tested range (4 cores, 12 jobs, 3 seeds).
checks.different_explanation: Part of the increase may come from how the simulator builds the skew: jobs J00-J08 go to core 0 by job ID, regardless of arrival time, so core 0 also gets most of the early arrivals. The size of the effect might then depend on this arrival pattern rather than only on the number of jobs per core.
checks.next_experiment: Use custom_skew with concentration 5, 7 and 10 (same seeds, quantum 2, penalty 0) and compare per_core avg_response. If imbalance is the cause, response time should grow steadily with concentration; if it jumps only when early arrivals are included, the arrival pattern is the main cause.
checks.comparison_with_original_prediction: I predicted that skewed placement would make per_core's average response time at least 25% worse while global stayed the same. The measured result (0.889 to 4.972 for per_core, 0.889 to 0.889 for global) agrees, because per_core has no work stealing and leaves cores 1-3 idle while core 0's queue is long, the wasted-cores effect from R01.

checks.what_the_results_show: K02 (F03): global makespan rose from 17.667 (C02) to 33.000 (C03) while per_core stayed at 42.667, so global still won under skew. K04 (F04): global makespan rose from 17.667 (C01) to 33.000 (C05) while per_core stayed at 20.000, and F05 shows per_core (20.000) now beats global (33.000). All four parts of H02 hold. A side effect was that global avg_response also rose (0.889 to 1.472) even though a job's first run is never a migration, because cores busy paying penalties delay other jobs.
checks.different_explanation: The large makespan increase may partly be an artefact of the model: it charges the full penalty on every core change, even when a job has waited so long that its cache would be cold anyway, and the penalty holds the core while giving no service. A real cache-reload cost would vary and could be smaller.
checks.next_experiment: Repeat C01/C05 with penalty 1 and 2 to find the crossover point where per_core starts to beat global under balanced placement, and repeat with quantum 4 plus penalty 4, which should cut global's migrations (3.667 instead of 13.333 per run) and shrink the penalty effect if migrations are the cause.
checks.comparison_with_original_prediction: I predicted that a 4-tick migration penalty would increase global's makespan but not per_core's, that per_core would match or beat global under balanced placement, and that global would still win under skew. The results agree on every point: global 17.667 to 33.000 in both pairs, per_core unchanged, per_core 20.000 vs global 33.000 in C05, and global 33.000 vs per_core 42.667 in C03. The reason is that global migrates about 14 times per run and each migration wastes core time, which only pays off when it fixes a large imbalance (R02).
